It was a helmet wired to a room-sized mechanical rig, suspended from the ceiling, and so heavy it had to be bolted to a frame—imagine playing a game while dangling in midair. The device tracked head movements and displayed primitive wireframe graphics. It was closer to a science experiment than a consumer product, but it laid the foundation for immersive gaming. Engineers had to invent algorithms to render visuals in real-time, decades before GPUs could handle the task. The concept was so futuristic it appeared in science fiction magazines as a potential future of entertainment. That early vision of VR created a roadmap for decades of innovation. It was a technology born before hardware could fully support it, a paradoxical start that still defines VR today.
